decks.title: National Income Aggregates — Part 1: The Eight Aggregates and National Income
goals: Define depreciation, net indirect taxes and net factor income from abroad
Convert between gross and net, market price and factor cost, and domestic and national aggregates
Explain domestic territory and normal residents
Calculate national income and per capita income

slides.heading: National Income Aggregates
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **eight aggregates**, the **three adjusting items**, and **national and per capita income**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the three adjusting items, the eight aggregates, domestic and national, working forwards and back, and per capita income
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When a country reports its income, it can mean several different totals. Some include worn-out machines, some include taxes inside prices, and some count income earned abroad. In this part we meet all eight of these totals, learn the three items that link them, and finish with national income and income per person.

slides.heading: Three items that link the aggregates
slides.body_md: Every aggregate name has three choices: **gross or net**, **market price or factor cost**, **domestic or national**.

rows: Fixed capital used up by wear and tear and expected obsolescence
Market price − net indirect taxes = factor cost
Factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad

visual.alt: Table of the three adjusting items: depreciation turns gross into net; net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies) turn market price into factor cost; net factor income from abroad turns domestic into national

slides.narration: Three items do all the work. Depreciation is the value of machines and buildings used up in a year, and it separates gross from net. Net indirect taxes, which are indirect taxes minus subsidies, separate market price from factor cost. Net factor income from abroad separates domestic from national.

slides.heading: The eight aggregates
slides.body_md: Combine the three choices and you get **eight** totals.

visual.alt: Grid of the eight aggregates: gross or net, domestic or national, each at market price and at factor cost; NDP at factor cost is domestic income and NNP at factor cost is national income
visual.caption: Three choices, eight combinations.

slides.narration: Pick gross or net, domestic or national, and market price or factor cost, and you have one of eight aggregates. Two of them have special names. Net domestic product at factor cost is domestic income, and net national product at factor cost is national income, the figure most often quoted.

slides.heading: Quick check: is factor cost always smaller?
slides.body_md: True or false: an aggregate at factor cost is always smaller than at market price.
slides.narration: Think about a country that pays out more in subsidies than it collects in indirect taxes.

slides.heading: Market price and factor cost
slides.body_md: Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies. When **subsidies exceed indirect taxes**, factor cost is the larger figure.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Phalguni Desh: NDP at market price 1800, indirect taxes 90, subsidies 150, so net indirect taxes are minus 60 and NDP at factor cost is 1860, larger than at market price
visual.caption: Subsidies larger than indirect taxes: factor cost above market price.

slides.narration: Indirect taxes such as goods and services tax push prices above what factors are paid. Subsidies pull prices below it. Usually taxes are larger, so market price is higher. But in imagined Phalguni Desh subsidies are larger, so net domestic product at factor cost, one thousand eight hundred and sixty crore, exceeds the market price figure.

slides.heading: Domestic territory and normal residents
slides.body_md: **Domestic** income is earned **inside the domestic territory**; **national** income is earned by **normal residents**, wherever they work.

rows: A foreign country's embassy in our capital
Our citizens' flats or firms in other countries
Our ships and aircraft operating abroad
Foreign ships passing through our waters
Our fishing vessels and oil rigs in our zone

visual.alt: Table of what lies inside the domestic territory (land, waters, airspace, our embassies abroad, our ships and aircraft, our fishing vessels and rigs) and what lies outside it (foreign embassies here, our property abroad, foreign ships, international organisations)

slides.narration: Domestic territory is wider than the map. It includes the country's embassies and military bases abroad, and its ships and aircraft operating between countries. A normal resident ordinarily lives in the country and has their centre of economic interest there. Domestic income follows the territory; national income follows the residents.

slides.heading: Net factor income from abroad
slides.body_md: NFIA = factor income received from abroad − factor income paid to non-residents. It can be **negative**.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Tirthapur: factor income received from abroad 260 (wages 180, property income 80); paid abroad 310 (wages 120, profits 190); net factor income from abroad is minus 50
visual.caption: NFIA = 260 − 310 = -50.

slides.narration: Residents of imagined Tirthapur earn two hundred and sixty crore abroad as wages and interest. Foreign workers and firms earn three hundred and ten crore inside Tirthapur. So net factor income from abroad is minus fifty crore, and Tirthapur's national product is smaller than its domestic product.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the net figure
slides.body_md: Find net factor income from abroad for imagined Tirthapur.
slides.narration: Add what residents earn abroad, add what non-residents earn here, and subtract the second from the first.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from GDP to national income
slides.body_md: Imagined Ambarpur: GDP at market price ₹4,800 crore. Find national income.
bullets: Step 1 — Gross to net: 4800 − depreciation 360 = **4,440**.
Step 2 — Market price to factor cost: − (470 − 50) = **4,020** (domestic income).
Step 3 — Domestic to national: + NFIA (-60) = **3,960**.
Step 4 — Write the answer with its name: NNP at factor cost, the national income.

visual.alt: Table of steps for imagined Ambarpur: GDP at market price 4800; minus depreciation 360 gives 4440; minus net indirect taxes 420 gives 4020; plus NFIA of minus 60 gives national income 3960

slides.narration: Start with four thousand eight hundred crore. Subtract depreciation of three hundred and sixty to reach the net figure. Subtract net indirect taxes of four hundred and twenty to reach domestic income, four thousand and twenty. Add net factor income from abroad, which is minus sixty, and national income is three thousand nine hundred and sixty crore.

slides.heading: Quick check: order the steps
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps from GDP at market price to national income.
slides.narration: Take away the worn-out capital first, then the taxes inside prices, then bring in income from abroad.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: working back to GDP
slides.body_md: Imagined Devgiri gives national income ₹2,700 crore. Find GDP at market price.
bullets: Step 1 — Remove NFIA: 2700 − 40 = **2,660** (NDP at factor cost).
Step 2 — Add net indirect taxes: + (330 − 50) = **2,940**.
Step 3 — Add depreciation: + 210 = **3,150**.
Step 4 — Every sign is the opposite of the forward direction.

visual.alt: Flow working back for imagined Devgiri: national income 2700, minus NFIA 40 gives NDP at factor cost 2660, plus net indirect taxes 280 gives NDP at market price 2940, plus depreciation 210 gives GDP at market price 3150
visual.caption: Working back: reverse each adjustment

slides.narration: Working backwards simply reverses each step. From national income of two thousand seven hundred, take away net factor income from abroad of forty. Add back net indirect taxes of two hundred and eighty. Add back depreciation of two hundred and ten. Gross domestic product at market price is three thousand one hundred and fifty crore.

slides.heading: National income and per capita income
slides.body_md: **National income** = NNP at factor cost. **Per capita income** = national income ÷ population.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Saptagiri: national income rises from 50000 to 54000 crore, but population rises from 2 to 2.25 crore, so per capita income falls from 25000 to 24000 rupees
visual.caption: National income up 8 per cent; population up 12.5 per cent.

slides.narration: National income is net national product at factor cost. To compare living standards, divide it by population to get per capita income. In imagined Saptagiri, national income rose eight per cent, but population rose faster, so income per person fell from twenty five thousand to twenty four thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the figure
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: national income is net national product at ___ cost.
slides.narration: Recall which of the two valuations excludes the taxes inside prices.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: per capita income
slides.body_md: Imagined Chandranagar: national income ₹63,000 crore, population 1.8 crore.
bullets: Step 1 — Write the formula: national income ÷ population.
Step 2 — Divide: 63,000 crore ÷ 1.8 crore.
Step 3 — The crores cancel: **₹35,000** per person.
Step 4 — Compare with other years or places, not with national income.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Chandranagar: national income 63000 crore rupees, population 1.8 crore, per capita income 35000 rupees

slides.narration: Imagined Chandranagar earns sixty three thousand crore rupees and has one point eight crore people. Dividing, the crores cancel and each person has thirty five thousand rupees on average. This average lets us compare Chandranagar with a larger or smaller place fairly.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Depreciation: gross to net. Net indirect taxes: market price to factor cost. NFIA: domestic to national.
Domestic income = NDP at factor cost; **national income = NNP at factor cost**.
Domestic follows the **territory**; national follows the **normal residents**.
Per capita income = national income ÷ population.

rows: Fixed capital used up by wear and tear and expected obsolescence
Market price − net indirect taxes = factor cost
Factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad

visual.alt: Table of the three adjusting items: depreciation turns gross into net; net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies) turn market price into factor cost; net factor income from abroad turns domestic into national

slides.narration: To sum up, three items link all eight aggregates. Depreciation separates gross from net, net indirect taxes separate market price from factor cost, and net factor income from abroad separates domestic from national. National income is net national product at factor cost, and dividing it by population gives per capita income.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **name** of each aggregate at every step of a calculation.
Keep the **sign** of NFIA; a negative NFIA makes national smaller than domestic.
Net indirect taxes = indirect taxes **minus** subsidies, never plus.
Embassies abroad are **inside** our domestic territory.
slides.narration: Four habits earn marks. Name every aggregate as you reach it, so the examiner can follow you. Keep the sign of net factor income from abroad. Remember that subsidies are subtracted from indirect taxes. And remember that a country's embassies abroad are part of its own domestic territory.

decks.title: National Income Aggregates — Part 2: Income Concepts, Real GDP and Welfare
goals: Calculate private income, personal income and personal disposable income
Calculate gross and net national disposable income
Distinguish real from nominal GDP and use the GDP deflator
Explain why GDP is an imperfect index of economic welfare

slides.heading: Income Concepts, Real GDP and Welfare
slides.body_md: Part 2 — from domestic income to **household income**, from nominal to **real GDP**, and **GDP and welfare**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: private income, personal and disposable income, national disposable income, real and nominal GDP, and GDP and welfare
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: National income tells us what the nation earns, but households care about what reaches them and what they can spend. In this part we follow income down to the household, add gifts from abroad to find disposable income, separate price rises from real growth, and ask whether a bigger economy always means better lives.

slides.heading: From domestic income to household income
slides.body_md: Each step **narrows** the income: first to the private sector, then to persons, then to what persons can freely use.

nodes.label: Income accruing to the private sector

visual.alt: Flow from NDP at factor cost to income accruing to the private sector, then private income, personal income and personal disposable income
visual.caption: From domestic income to household income

slides.narration: Start with domestic income. Remove what government departments and public enterprises keep, and you have income accruing to the private sector. Add income from abroad and transfers to reach private income. Remove what companies keep or pay in tax to reach personal income. Remove personal taxes, fees and fines to reach personal disposable income.

slides.heading: Private income
slides.body_md: Private income = income from domestic product accruing to the private sector + NFIA + current transfers from government + net current transfers from abroad + interest on national debt.

visual.alt: Table for imagined Lohitpur: income accruing to the private sector 8300; adding NFIA, transfers from government and from abroad and interest on national debt gives private income 9000; subtracting corporate saving and corporation tax gives personal income 7900; subtracting direct taxes and fees gives personal disposable income 7100

slides.narration: Private income counts every rupee the private sector receives, whether earned or not. Besides factor income, it includes pensions and scholarships from the government, gifts from abroad, and interest the government pays on its debt, which is treated as a transfer. It excludes income that government departments earn from their own property and businesses.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: private income in imagined Lohitpur
slides.body_md: Domestic income ₹9,000 crore. Find private income step by step.
bullets: Step 1 — Private share of domestic income: 9,000 − 400 − 300 = **8,300**.
Step 2 — Add NFIA 150 and transfers from government 250.
Step 3 — Add net transfers from abroad 120 and interest on national debt 180.
Step 4 — Private income = **9,000** (₹ crore).

visual.alt: Table of imagined Lohitpur private income: private share 8300 plus NFIA 150, transfers from government 250, transfers from abroad 120 and interest on national debt 180 gives 9000

slides.narration: In imagined Lohitpur, domestic income is nine thousand crore. Government departments earn four hundred from their property and public enterprises save three hundred, so the private share is eight thousand three hundred. Adding income from abroad, transfers from the government and from abroad, and interest on national debt gives private income of nine thousand crore.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the income
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: personal income minus direct taxes and fees gives personal ___ income.
slides.narration: Think of the income a family is free to spend or save.

slides.heading: Personal and personal disposable income
slides.body_md: Personal income = private income − corporate saving − corporation tax. PDI = personal income − direct personal taxes − fees and fines.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Lohitpur: private income 9000 minus corporate saving 600 and corporation tax 500 gives personal income 7900; minus direct taxes 700 and fees 100 gives personal disposable income 7100

slides.narration: Companies keep part of their profit and pay corporation tax, so that money never reaches persons. Subtracting both gives personal income, seven thousand nine hundred crore. Households then pay income tax, fees and fines, and what is left, seven thousand one hundred crore, is personal disposable income, which they can spend or save as they like.

slides.heading: Quick check: what can households use?
slides.body_md: True or false: personal disposable income is what households can divide freely between consumption and saving.
slides.narration: Ask what remains once companies and the government have taken their shares.

slides.heading: National disposable income
slides.body_md: Net NDI = NNP at market price + net current transfers from abroad. Gross NDI = net NDI + depreciation.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Mandakini: NNP at market price 5200 plus net current transfers 140 gives net national disposable income 5340; adding depreciation 400 gives gross national disposable income 5740

slides.narration: National disposable income looks at the whole nation, not just households. To net national product at market price, add net current transfers from the rest of the world, such as gifts and remittances. In imagined Mandakini that gives five thousand three hundred and forty crore. Add depreciation for the gross figure, five thousand seven hundred and forty.

slides.heading: Nominal and real GDP
slides.body_md: **Nominal GDP** uses **current prices**; **real GDP** uses **base-year prices**, so it moves only when output moves.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Ketakipur: base year rice 100 at 20 and cloth 50 at 40; current year rice 120 at 25 and cloth 60 at 50; nominal GDP 4000 and 6000; real GDP 4000 and 4800

slides.narration: Imagined Ketakipur grows rice and cloth. Valued at this year's prices, its output is six thousand. But some of that rise is only prices. Valued at base-year prices, the same quantities are worth four thousand eight hundred. That second figure, real gross domestic product, tells us how much more was actually produced.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the GDP deflator
slides.body_md: Ketakipur: nominal GDP 6,000, real GDP 4,800. Find the deflator and the real growth rate.
bullets: Step 2 — Prices are 25 per cent above the base year.
Step 3 — Real growth = (4800 − 4000) ÷ 4000 × 100 = **20 per cent**.
Step 4 — Nominal growth was 50 per cent; the rest is price rise.

slides.body_md: GDP is an **imperfect** index of welfare because of **distribution**, **non-monetary exchanges** and **externalities**.

slides.narration: Economic welfare means the well-being people get from goods and services. A larger real gross domestic product can raise it, but three things get in the way. If the gains go to a few, most people may not benefit. Unpaid work at home is left out. And harms or benefits that nobody pays for are not counted.

columns:
**Negative externality**

- Harm to others, no compensation
- e.g. a tannery polluting a river
- Not deducted: GDP **overstates** welfare

**Positive externality**

- Benefit to others, no payment
- e.g. a garden freshening a street
- Not added: GDP **understates** welfare

A family garden freshens the air of the whole street

slides.narration: An externality is an effect on others that no market price records. A tannery that pollutes a river raises output, which raises gross domestic product, but nobody deducts the harm to fishing families, so welfare is overstated. sections.heading: 1. The three adjusting items
sections.body_md:
- **Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital)**: the fall in value of fixed assets in a year from normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence. Gross − depreciation = net.
- **Net indirect taxes** = indirect taxes − subsidies. Market price − net indirect taxes = factor cost. If subsidies exceed indirect taxes, net indirect taxes are negative and factor cost exceeds market price.
- **Net factor income from abroad (NFIA)** = factor income received by normal residents from abroad − factor income paid to non-residents. Domestic + NFIA = national. Its parts: net compensation of employees, net property and entrepreneurial income, net retained earnings of resident companies abroad.

sections.heading: 3. Domestic territory, normal residents and per capita income
sections.body_md:
- **Domestic territory**: political frontiers, territorial waters and airspace, plus embassies, consulates and military bases abroad, ships and aircraft operating abroad, and fishing vessels and rigs in the country's zone. Foreign embassies and international organisations located here are excluded.
- **Normal resident**: a person or institution that ordinarily resides in the country and whose centre of economic interest is there. Foreign tourists, crews and diplomats are not normal residents.
- **Per capita income** = national income ÷ population. It falls if population grows faster than national income. Imagined Saptagiri: ₹25,000 to ₹24,000 although national income rose 8 per cent.

sections.heading: 4. Private, personal and disposable income
sections.body_md:
- **Income from domestic product accruing to the private sector** = NDP at factor cost − property and entrepreneurial income of government departments − saving of non-departmental public enterprises.
- **Private income** = that + NFIA + current transfers from government + net current transfers from abroad + interest on national debt (a transfer).
- **Personal income** = private income − corporate saving (undistributed profits) − corporation tax.
- **Personal disposable income** = personal income − direct personal taxes − miscellaneous receipts of government (fees, fines).
- **Net national disposable income** = NNP at market price + net current transfers from abroad; **gross** = net + depreciation.
- Imagined Lohitpur (₹ crore): 8,300 → 9,000 → 7,900 → 7,100. Imagined Mandakini: net NDI 5,340, gross 5,740.

sections.heading: 6. GDP and welfare
sections.body_md:
- **Economic welfare**: well-being from goods and services that can be measured in money.
- **Distribution of income**: GDP shows the total, not who gets it; if gains go to a few, most people may not be better off.
- **Non-monetary exchanges**: unpaid household work, self-produced goods and barter are largely excluded, so GDP understates welfare.
- **Externalities**: harms (pollution) are not deducted and benefits (a public garden) are not added, so GDP can overstate or understate welfare.
- Conclusion: real GDP is a useful but **incomplete** index of welfare.

- 3 marks: a calculation in steps with each aggregate named, or three points.

questions.stem_md: An accountant in an imagined Ambarpur ministry explains the item "consumption of fixed capital" in the national accounts. It means

options.text_md: the total value of new machines bought by firms in a year
the fall in the value of fixed assets through normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence in a year
the value of raw materials used up in production
the loss of assets in an unexpected flood or fire

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the fall in the value of fixed assets through normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence in a year. Consumption of fixed capital (depreciation) is the expected loss in value of fixed assets from normal use and obsolescence. New machines are gross investment; raw materials are intermediate consumption; unexpected losses are capital losses, not depreciation.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Ambarpur, the government collects indirect taxes on goods and also pays subsidies to producers. Net indirect taxes are

options.text_md: indirect taxes plus subsidies
direct taxes minus subsidies
indirect taxes minus direct taxes
indirect taxes minus subsidies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** indirect taxes minus subsidies. Net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies. Indirect taxes raise market prices above factor cost, while subsidies lower them, so the net figure is what separates market price from factor cost.

questions.stem_md: A teacher in imagined Tirthapur asks her class to define net factor income from abroad. Which answer is correct?

options.text_md: Factor income earned by normal residents from abroad minus factor income earned by non-residents in the domestic territory
Exports of goods minus imports of goods
Gifts received from abroad minus gifts sent abroad
Factor income earned within the domestic territory minus depreciation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Factor income earned by normal residents from abroad minus factor income earned by non-residents in the domestic territory. Net factor income from abroad is factor income received from the rest of the world by normal residents minus factor income paid to non-residents. Net exports and net gifts are not factor incomes; the last option mixes up domestic income with depreciation.

questions.stem_md: For imagined Ambarpur, which relationship links gross national product to gross domestic product at market price?

options.text_md: GNP at market price = GDP at market price − depreciation
GNP at market price = GDP at market price − net indirect taxes
GNP at market price = GDP at market price + net factor income from abroad
GNP at market price = GDP at market price + net indirect taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** GNP at market price = GDP at market price + net factor income from abroad. Moving from domestic to national adds net factor income from abroad. Subtracting depreciation turns gross into net, and subtracting net indirect taxes turns market price into factor cost.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Ambarpur reports (₹ crore): GDP at market price 4,800, depreciation 360, indirect taxes 470, subsidies 50, net factor income from abroad (−) 60. What is its national income?

options.text_md: ₹4,020 crore
₹4,380 crore
₹3,960 crore
₹3,860 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹3,960 crore. National income = NNP at factor cost = 4800 − 360 − (470 − 50) − 60 = 3960. 4,020 is the domestic figure (NFIA left out); 4,380 keeps net indirect taxes; the last figure treats subsidies as a tax.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Devgiri has national income ₹2,700 crore, net factor income from abroad ₹40 crore, depreciation ₹210 crore and net indirect taxes ₹280 crore. Its GDP at market price is

options.text_md: ₹3,150 crore
₹3,230 crore
₹2,940 crore
₹2,910 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹3,150 crore. Work back: NDP at factor cost = 2700 − 40 = 2660; add net indirect taxes: 2660 + 280 = 2940; add depreciation: 2940 + 210 = 3150. Adding the NFIA instead of subtracting it gives 3230.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Phalguni Desh, subsidies (₹150 crore) are larger than indirect taxes (₹90 crore). Which statement about its domestic product follows?

options.text_md: NDP at factor cost is smaller than NDP at market price
NDP at factor cost equals NDP at market price
NDP at factor cost cannot be found without depreciation
NDP at factor cost is greater than NDP at market price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** NDP at factor cost is greater than NDP at market price. Net indirect taxes = 90 − 150 = -60, a negative number. Factor cost = market price − net indirect taxes = 1800 + 60 = 1860, so factor cost exceeds market price. Depreciation is already excluded from both net figures.

questions.stem_md: Which income is included in the domestic product of an imagined country Ambarpur?

options.text_md: Rent earned by an Ambarpur family from a flat it owns abroad
Salaries paid to Ambarpur staff working in Ambarpur's embassy in a foreign capital
Profit earned by an Ambarpur bank from its branch in another country
Salaries of a foreign country's diplomats working in its embassy in Ambarpur

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Salaries paid to Ambarpur staff working in Ambarpur's embassy in a foreign capital. A country's embassies abroad are part of its domestic territory, so salaries earned there count in its domestic product. Rent and branch profits from abroad are factor income from abroad (national, not domestic); a foreign embassy inside Ambarpur is foreign territory.

questions.stem_md: Which person is a normal resident of the imagined country Tirthapur?

options.text_md: A Tirthapur engineer who has worked on a two-year project abroad and keeps her home and family in Tirthapur
A foreign tourist spending three weeks in Tirthapur
A foreign ship's crew docked at a Tirthapur port for a month
A foreign diplomat posted in Tirthapur for three years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A Tirthapur engineer who has worked on a two-year project abroad and keeps her home and family in Tirthapur. A normal resident ordinarily lives in a country and has her centre of economic interest there. The engineer keeps her home and interests in Tirthapur. Tourists, foreign crews and foreign diplomats remain residents of their own countries.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The gross national product of imagined Tirthapur is less than its gross domestic product.

**Reason (R):** Factor income paid to non-residents by Tirthapur is greater than the factor income its normal residents receive from abroad.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A. Received 260 and paid 310 give net factor income from abroad of -50; adding a negative number to GDP makes GNP smaller.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Net domestic product is always smaller than gross domestic product.

**Reason (R):** Net domestic product includes the value of machines that wear out during the year.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: depreciation is a positive amount, so subtracting it makes the net figure smaller. R is false: the net figure is obtained by removing the value of fixed capital used up, not by including it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In every economy, an aggregate at factor cost is smaller than the same aggregate at market price.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Factor cost is smaller only when indirect taxes exceed subsidies. In imagined Phalguni Desh, subsidies are larger, so NDP at factor cost (1860) exceeds NDP at market price (1800).

questions.stem_md: National income is the net national product at ___ cost.
questions.solution_md: National income is NNP at factor cost: the factor incomes earned by normal residents in a year.

questions.stem_md: Normal residents of imagined Tirthapur earn wages of ₹180 crore and interest and dividends of ₹80 crore from abroad. Non-residents earn wages of ₹120 crore and profits of ₹190 crore in Tirthapur. Find net factor income from abroad (in ₹ crore; give a negative number if it is negative).
For imagined Ambarpur (₹ crore): GDP at market price 4,800, indirect taxes 470, subsidies 50, net factor income from abroad (−) 60. Find GNP at factor cost (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: GNP at factor cost = GDP at market price − net indirect taxes + NFIA = 4800 − (470 − 50) − 60 = 4320, that is ₹4,320 crore.

questions.stem_md: Match each conversion between aggregates in the imagined Ambarpur accounts with the item that makes it.

options.text_md: Gross to net
Market price to factor cost
Domestic to national
Factor cost to market price

match_right.text_md: Add net factor income from abroad

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each word in an aggregate's name has one adjusting item: gross or net (depreciation), market price or factor cost (net indirect taxes), domestic or national (net factor income from abroad).

questions.stem_md: Starting from GDP at market price, arrange the steps an imagined Ambarpur statistician follows to reach national income.

options.text_md: Add net factor income from abroad to get NNP at factor cost
Start with GDP at market price
Subtract net indirect taxes to get NDP at factor cost
Subtract depreciation to get NDP at market price

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Gross to net, market price to factor cost, then domestic to national. Other orders give the same final figure, but this order passes through NDP at factor cost, the domestic income on which national income is built.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Distinguish domestic income from national income, mentioning the item that links them, with reference to an imagined trading country.
questions.solution_md: Territory versus residents, linked by NFIA.

answer.model_answer_md: **Domestic income** (NDP at factor cost) is the factor income earned **within the domestic territory**, by residents and non-residents alike. **National income** (NNP at factor cost) is the factor income earned by **normal residents**, at home or abroad. They differ by **net factor income from abroad**.

marking_scheme.step: National income: by normal residents; linked by NFIA

questions.stem_md: Explain why GDP of an imagined country valued at market price differs from GDP at factor cost.
questions.solution_md: Indirect taxes raise, subsidies lower market prices; the gap is net indirect taxes.

answer.model_answer_md: Market prices include **indirect taxes** such as GST, which raise prices above what factors are paid, and are reduced by **subsidies**, which lower them. So GDP at factor cost = GDP at market price **− (indirect taxes − subsidies)**, that is, minus **net indirect taxes**.

marking_scheme.step: Role of indirect taxes and subsidies

questions.stem_md: State the difference between gross and net aggregates, and why the net figure is a better measure of what an imagined economy can use.
questions.solution_md: Depreciation included or excluded; net shows what is truly available.

answer.model_answer_md: A **gross** aggregate includes **depreciation**, the value of fixed capital used up during the year; a **net** aggregate **excludes** it. The net figure is better because that part of gross output only **replaces worn-out machines** and is not available for consumption or new investment.

questions.stem_md: Name the components of net factor income from abroad and give an example of one from an imagined Indian state with many workers in the Gulf.
questions.solution_md: Three components with one example.

answer.model_answer_md: Net factor income from abroad includes (1) net **compensation of employees**, (2) net **property and entrepreneurial income** (rent, interest, dividends, profits) and (3) net **retained earnings** of resident companies abroad. Example: **wages sent home** by residents working temporarily in Gulf countries.

questions.stem_md: For imagined Ambarpur (₹ crore): GDP at market price 4,800, depreciation 360, indirect taxes 470, subsidies 50, net factor income from abroad (−) 60. Find NDP at market price, GDP at factor cost and NNP at market price.
questions.solution_md: Apply one adjustment for each change of word in the name.

answer.model_answer_md:
**NDP at market price** = GDP at market price − depreciation = 4800 − 360 = **₹4,440 crore**.
**GDP at factor cost** = GDP at market price − net indirect taxes = 4800 − (470 − 50) = **₹4,380 crore**.
**NNP at market price** = GDP at market price − depreciation + NFIA = 4800 − 360 − 60 = **₹4,380 crore**.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Devgiri reports national income ₹2,700 crore, net factor income from abroad ₹40 crore, depreciation ₹210 crore, indirect taxes ₹330 crore and subsidies ₹50 crore. Work back to its GDP at market price, showing each step.
questions.solution_md: Reverse the three adjustments one at a time.

answer.model_answer_md:
Step 1: NDP at factor cost = NNP at factor cost − NFIA = 2700 − 40 = **2,660**.
Step 2: NDP at market price = NDP at factor cost + net indirect taxes = 2660 + (330 − 50) = **2,940**.
Step 3: GDP at market price = NDP at market price + depreciation = 2940 + 210 = **₹3,150 crore**. Each step reverses one adjustment.

questions.stem_md: Explain briefly the three items used to move between the eight national income aggregates of an imagined economy.
questions.solution_md: Depreciation, net indirect taxes, NFIA, each with its conversion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Depreciation** (consumption of fixed capital): subtracted to go from **gross to net**.
2. **Net indirect taxes** (indirect taxes − subsidies): subtracted to go from **market price to factor cost**.
3. **Net factor income from abroad** (factor income received from abroad − paid abroad): added to go from **domestic to national**.
Combining them links any aggregate, such as GDP at market price, to national income.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about imagined Ambarpur (₹ crore): GDP at market price 4,800, depreciation 360, indirect taxes 470, subsidies 50, factor income received from abroad 140, factor income paid abroad 200. [2 + 3]

(a) Find net indirect taxes and net factor income from abroad. [2]
(b) Find NDP at factor cost, GNP at market price and national income. [3]
questions.solution_md: Net items first, then one adjustment per change of word.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Net indirect taxes** = indirect taxes − subsidies = 470 − 50 = **₹420 crore**. **Net factor income from abroad** = received − paid = 140 − 200 = **₹-60 crore**, negative because non-residents earn more in Ambarpur than its residents earn abroad.
(b) **NDP at factor cost** = GDP at market price − depreciation − net indirect taxes = 4800 − 360 − 420 = **₹4,020 crore**, the income earned inside the territory. **GNP at market price** = GDP at market price + NFIA = 4800 + (-60) = **₹4,740 crore**. **National income** = NDP at factor cost + NFIA = 4020 + (-60) = **₹3,960 crore**, the factor income earned by normal residents.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined country Ambarpur. [2 + 3]

(a) Explain the terms domestic territory and normal resident. [2]
(b) State, with a reason, whether each income is part of Ambarpur's domestic income, its national income, or both: (i) wages of Ambarpur nurses in a foreign hospital; (ii) profit of a foreign bank's branch in Ambarpur; (iii) salary of an Ambarpur clerk in Ambarpur's embassy abroad. [3]
questions.solution_md: Define both terms; classify each income by where it is earned and who earns it.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Domestic territory** is the economic territory of a country: its land, territorial waters and airspace, plus its **embassies, consulates and military bases abroad** and its ships and aircraft operating abroad. A **normal resident** is a person or institution that **ordinarily lives** in the country and whose **centre of economic interest** lies there.
(b) (i) **National only**: the nurses are normal residents, but they earn **outside** the domestic territory. (ii) **Domestic only**: the profit arises **inside** Ambarpur but goes to a **non-resident** bank. (iii) **Both**: the embassy is part of Ambarpur's domestic territory and the clerk is a normal resident, so the salary counts in domestic and in national income.

questions.stem_md: A newspaper in an imagined state reports its per capita income. Per capita income means

options.text_md: national income divided by the number of workers
national income divided by the population
GDP divided by the number of households
personal income of the richest tenth of people

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** national income divided by the population. Per capita income is the average income per person: national income divided by total population. Dividing by workers or households gives other averages.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Chandranagar has national income of ₹63,000 crore and a population of 1.8 crore. Its per capita income is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹35,000. Per capita income = ₹63,000 crore ÷ 1.8 crore persons = ₹35,000. The crores cancel, so the answer is in rupees per person.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Saptagiri, national income rises from ₹50,000 crore to ₹54,000 crore while population rises from 2 crore to 2.25 crore. What happens to per capita income?

options.text_md: It rises from ₹25,000 to ₹26,000
It stays the same
It rises by 8 per cent
It falls from ₹25,000 to ₹24,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It falls from ₹25,000 to ₹24,000. Per capita income falls: 50000 ÷ 2 = 25000, but 54000 ÷ 2.25 = 24000. Population grew faster than national income (8 per cent).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Per capita income is a better guide than national income for comparing the average living standard of two countries.

**Reason (R):** National income does not take account of depreciation of fixed assets.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: dividing by population allows for differences in the size of countries. R is false: national income is a net figure, so depreciation has already been subtracted from it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined hill state has national income of ₹84,000 crore and a population of 2 crore. Find its per capita income (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Per capita income = ₹84,000 crore ÷ 2 crore persons = ₹42,000 per person.

questions.stem_md: Why can per capita income of an imagined country fall in a year when its national income rises?
questions.solution_md: Population growth faster than income growth.

answer.model_answer_md: Per capita income = national income ÷ population. If **population grows faster** than national income, the average falls. In imagined Saptagiri, national income rose **8 per cent** but population rose more, so per capita income fell from **₹25,000 to ₹24,000**.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Saptagiri's national income was ₹50,000 crore with 2 crore people last year, and is ₹54,000 crore with 2.25 crore people this year. Calculate per capita income in both years and comment.
questions.solution_md: Two divisions and a comment comparing growth rates.

answer.model_answer_md: Last year: 50,000 ÷ 2 = **₹25,000**. This year: 54,000 ÷ 2.25 = **₹24,000**. Although national income rose by **8 per cent**, population rose by 12.5 per cent, so the **average person is poorer**. Growth in total income is not enough; it must outpace population growth to raise living standards.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes private income in the accounts of an imagined economy?

options.text_md: Factor income earned only by government departments
Income left with households after paying all taxes
The value of goods produced by private firms
Factor income and current transfers from all sources received by the private sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Factor income and current transfers from all sources received by the private sector. Private income covers the factor income accruing to the private sector from home and abroad plus the current transfers it receives (from government and the rest of the world, including interest on national debt). Income after taxes is personal disposable income.

questions.stem_md: To move from private income to personal income for imagined Lohitpur, a statistician must subtract

options.text_md: direct personal taxes and fees
depreciation and net indirect taxes
corporate saving and corporation tax
current transfers from abroad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** corporate saving and corporation tax. Personal income = private income − corporate saving (undistributed profits) − corporation tax, because these belong to companies and never reach persons. Personal taxes are subtracted later to reach personal disposable income.

questions.stem_md: Interest paid by the imagined government of Lohitpur on loans taken to meet a war expense is treated as

options.text_md: a factor income included in national income
a transfer included in private income but not in national income
part of corporation tax
a capital receipt of the private sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a transfer included in private income but not in national income. Interest on national debt is usually treated as a transfer payment, since the loans paid for consumption and created no productive asset. It is excluded from national income but included in private income.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Lohitpur has personal income ₹7,900 crore, direct personal taxes ₹700 crore and fees and fines paid to government ₹100 crore. Its personal disposable income is

options.text_md: ₹7,100 crore
₹7,200 crore
₹8,000 crore
₹6,600 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹7,100 crore. PDI = 7900 − 700 − 100 = 7100. Leaving out fees and fines gives 7200; corporation tax was already removed when personal income was found.

questions.stem_md: Net national disposable income of an imagined country is

options.text_md: NNP at factor cost minus direct taxes
NNP at market price plus net current transfers from the rest of the world
GDP at market price plus depreciation
personal income plus corporate saving

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** NNP at market price plus net current transfers from the rest of the world. Net national disposable income = NNP at market price + net current transfers from abroad. It is the income the whole nation can use for consumption and saving.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Mandakini has NNP at market price ₹5,200 crore, net current transfers from abroad ₹140 crore and depreciation ₹400 crore. Its gross national disposable income is

options.text_md: ₹5,340 crore
₹5,600 crore
₹5,460 crore
₹5,740 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹5,740 crore. Net national disposable income = 5200 + 140 = 5340; gross = 5340 + 400 = 5740. 5,340 is the net figure; the others leave out or subtract the transfers.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Personal income of an economy is smaller than its private income.

**Reason (R):** Part of private income is kept by companies as undistributed profits or paid as corporation tax, and never reaches persons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A. In imagined Lohitpur, 9000 − 600 − 500 = 7900.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gifts sent home by residents working abroad are excluded from national disposable income.

**Reason (R):** National disposable income counts only factor incomes earned within the domestic territory.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Such remittances are current transfers from abroad and are included in national disposable income, which adds net current transfers to NNP at market price; it is not limited to domestic factor income.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Personal disposable income is the income that households of an imagined country can divide freely between consumption and saving.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. After companies keep their share and households pay direct taxes, fees and fines, the remainder is personal disposable income, which households spend or save as they choose.

questions.stem_md: Personal income minus direct personal taxes minus miscellaneous receipts of government gives personal ___ income.
questions.solution_md: The result is personal disposable income.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Lohitpur (₹ crore): NDP at factor cost 9,000; income from property and entrepreneurship of government departments 400; saving of non-departmental public enterprises 300; net factor income from abroad 150; current transfers from government 250; net current transfers from abroad 120; interest on national debt 180. Find private income (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: Income from domestic product accruing to the private sector = 9000 − 400 − 300 = 8300. Private income = 8300 + 150 + 250 + 120 + 180 = 9000, that is ₹9,000 crore.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Rewa Desh (₹ crore): GDP at market price 6,000, net factor income from abroad (−) 80, net current transfers from abroad 220, depreciation 500. Find net national disposable income (in ₹ crore).
Distinguish private income from personal income for an imagined economy with many large companies.
questions.solution_md: Private sector versus persons; corporate saving and tax.

answer.model_answer_md: **Private income** is all factor income and current transfers received by the **private sector**, including companies. **Personal income** is the part that actually reaches **persons and households**: private income minus **corporate saving** and **corporation tax**, which stay with or go from companies.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish gross national disposable income from net national disposable income for an imagined country.
questions.solution_md: Net versus gross, differing by depreciation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Net national disposable income** = NNP at market price + net current transfers from abroad. **Gross national disposable income** = net national disposable income **+ depreciation** (or GNP at market price + net current transfers). The gross figure includes the part needed to replace worn-out capital.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Lohitpur has private income ₹9,000 crore, corporate saving ₹600 crore, corporation tax ₹500 crore, direct personal taxes ₹700 crore and fees and fines ₹100 crore. Find personal income and personal disposable income, stating why each item is subtracted.
questions.solution_md: Two subtractions, each with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **Personal income** = 9000 − 600 − 500 = **₹7,900 crore**: undistributed profits and corporation tax belong to companies and never reach persons. **Personal disposable income** = 7900 − 700 − 100 = **₹7,100 crore**: personal taxes, fees and fines must be paid to the government, so they are not free for spending or saving.

questions.stem_md: Explain how private income, personal income and personal disposable income are related in the accounts of an imagined economy.
questions.solution_md: Three concepts, each narrower than the last.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Private income** is the widest: factor income from the domestic product accruing to the private sector, plus NFIA and current transfers (including interest on national debt).
2. **Personal income** = private income − corporate saving − corporation tax, the part reaching persons.
3. **Personal disposable income** = personal income − direct personal taxes − fees and fines, what households can spend or save.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about imagined Lohitpur (₹ crore): NDP at factor cost 9,000; income from property and entrepreneurship of government departments 400; saving of non-departmental public enterprises 300; net factor income from abroad 150; current transfers from government 250; net current transfers from abroad 120; interest on national debt 180; corporate saving 600; corporation tax 500. [3 + 2]

(a) Find private income. [3]
(b) Find personal income and explain why it is smaller than private income. [2]
questions.solution_md: Private-sector domestic income, then additions; then corporate deductions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) First find the **income from domestic product accruing to the private sector** = NDP at factor cost − government departments' property and entrepreneurial income − saving of non-departmental enterprises = 9000 − 400 − 300 = **8,300**. Then **private income** = 8300 + NFIA 150 + transfers from government 250 + net transfers from abroad 120 + interest on national debt 180 = **₹9,000 crore**.
(b) **Personal income** = 9000 − 600 − 500 = **₹7,900 crore**. It is smaller because companies **keep undistributed profits** and **pay corporation tax**; both are part of private income but never reach households.

questions.stem_md: Which formula gives the GDP deflator used by an imagined central statistics office?

options.text_md: (Nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100
(Real GDP ÷ nominal GDP) × 100
Nominal GDP − real GDP
(Real GDP ÷ population) × 100

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** (Nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100. The GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100. It measures how much the general price level of output has changed from the base year.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Shivalik Pradesh has nominal GDP of ₹9,900 crore and real GDP of ₹9,000 crore. Its GDP deflator is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 110. Deflator = 9900 ÷ 9000 × 100 = 110: prices are 10 per cent above the base year. Inverting the ratio gives about 90.91.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Ketakipur, nominal GDP rises from ₹4,000 crore to ₹6,000 crore while real GDP (base-year prices) rises to ₹4,800 crore. How much of the rise reflects more goods produced?

options.text_md: A 50 per cent rise in output
No rise in output at all
A 20 per cent rise in output; the rest is higher prices
A 125 per cent rise in output

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A 20 per cent rise in output; the rest is higher prices. Real GDP rose from 4000 to 4800, which is 20 per cent: that is the growth in output. Nominal GDP rose 50 per cent; the extra came from prices rising by a quarter.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rise in nominal GDP does not necessarily mean that more goods and services have been produced.

**Reason (R):** Nominal GDP is valued at current prices, so it rises when prices rise even if output is unchanged.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: nominal GDP mixes changes in quantity with changes in price, so only real GDP shows the change in output.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state has nominal GDP of ₹7,560 crore and a GDP deflator of 108. Find its real GDP (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: Real GDP = nominal GDP × 100 ÷ deflator = 7560 × 100 ÷ 108 = 7000, that is ₹7,000 crore.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish nominal GDP from real GDP for an imagined country with rising prices.
questions.solution_md: Current versus constant prices.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nominal GDP** values the year's output at **current prices**, so it rises with both output and prices. **Real GDP** values the same output at **constant base-year prices**, so it changes **only when output changes**. With rising prices, nominal GDP exceeds real GDP.

questions.stem_md: What does a GDP deflator of 110 tell an analyst about the economy of imagined Kesari Ghat?
questions.solution_md: Prices 10 per cent above the base year.

answer.model_answer_md: It shows that the **general price level** of goods and services produced is **10 per cent higher** than in the base year. Nominal GDP must be divided by 1.1 to remove this price effect and find **real GDP**.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Ketakipur produces rice and cloth. Base year: 100 units of rice at ₹20, 50 units of cloth at ₹40. Current year: 120 units of rice at ₹25, 60 units of cloth at ₹50. Find nominal and real GDP of the current year and the GDP deflator.
questions.solution_md: Current quantities at current and at base prices, then the ratio.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nominal GDP** (current prices) = 120 × 25 + 60 × 50 = **₹6,000**. **Real GDP** (base-year prices) = 120 × 20 + 60 × 40 = **₹4,800**. **GDP deflator** = 6000 ÷ 4800 × 100 = **125**, so prices have risen by a quarter since the base year.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Kesari Ghat's nominal GDP rose from ₹2,000 crore (base year, deflator 100) to ₹2,310 crore, with the deflator now 110. By what percentage did real GDP grow? Comment on the result.
questions.solution_md: Deflate, then compare with the base year.

answer.model_answer_md: Real GDP now = 2310 × 100 ÷ 110 = **₹2,100 crore**. In the base year real and nominal GDP are equal at 2,000. Real growth = (2100 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = **5 per cent**. Nominal GDP rose by 15.5 per cent, but most of that came from **higher prices**; output grew only 5 per cent.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about imagined Ketakipur, which produces only rice and cloth. Base year: 100 units of rice at ₹20 and 50 units of cloth at ₹40. Current year: 120 units at ₹25 and 60 units at ₹50. [2 + 3]

(a) Distinguish real GDP from nominal GDP. [2]
(b) Calculate the growth of nominal and of real GDP, and explain which better shows the change in output. [3]
questions.solution_md: Definitions; three totals; two growth rates; judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Nominal GDP** values output at the **prices of the same year**; **real GDP** values it at **constant base-year prices**, so it moves only when **quantities** move.
(b) Base-year GDP = 100 × 20 + 50 × 40 = **₹4,000** (nominal and real are equal in the base year). Current nominal GDP = 120 × 25 + 60 × 50 = **₹6,000**, a rise of **50 per cent**. Current real GDP = 120 × 20 + 60 × 40 = **₹4,800**, a rise of **20 per cent**. **Real GDP** is the better guide: output grew by a fifth, while the rest of the nominal rise reflects prices that went up by a quarter.

questions.stem_md: Real GDP of an imagined country rises by 6 per cent, but almost all the gain goes to a few rich families. Which limitation of GDP as a welfare index does this show?

options.text_md: Distribution of income
Non-monetary exchanges
Externalities
Depreciation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Distribution of income. GDP shows the total, not how it is shared. If the gain goes to a few, the welfare of most people may not improve, so distribution is the limitation shown.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined hill village, families grow vegetables for their own kitchens and help each other build houses without payment. These activities are mostly left out of GDP. Which limitation does this illustrate?

options.text_md: Negative externalities
Distribution of income
Price changes
Non-monetary exchanges

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Non-monetary exchanges. Activities that are not bought and sold for money are hard to value and are largely left out, so GDP understates the welfare they create.

questions.stem_md: A tannery in an imagined river town raises output but pollutes the water used by fishing families downstream, without paying them. In national accounting terms the pollution is

options.text_md: a positive externality added to GDP
a negative externality not deducted from GDP
a transfer payment
part of depreciation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a negative externality not deducted from GDP. Harm caused to others without compensation is a negative externality. GDP counts the tannery's output but does not subtract the harm, so it overstates welfare.

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined town plants a large garden that freshens the air for the whole street. How does GDP treat this benefit to the neighbours?

options.text_md: It ignores it, so GDP understates welfare
It adds its full value to GDP
It subtracts it as depreciation
It counts it as a factor income of the neighbours

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It ignores it, so GDP understates welfare. The neighbours' benefit is a positive externality: nobody pays for it, so it has no market value and is left out of GDP, which therefore understates welfare.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** GDP may overstate the welfare of people living near a busy industrial belt.

**Reason (R):** GDP counts the factories' output but does not deduct the cost of the pollution they impose on others.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: negative externalities harm welfare but are not subtracted from GDP.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A higher real GDP always means that the people of an imagined country are better off.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Welfare also depends on how income is distributed, on unpaid non-market activities and on externalities such as pollution, none of which GDP fully captures.

questions.stem_md: Name any two limitations of GDP as an index of economic welfare and explain one of them with an example from an imagined city.
questions.solution_md: Two named, one explained with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Two limitations: **distribution of income** and **externalities** (also non-monetary exchanges). Example of externalities: a city's new power plant raises GDP, but its **smoke harms residents' health**; this cost is **not deducted** from GDP, so GDP overstates welfare.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined countries, Rajgarh and Sonagarh, have the same real GDP and population. In Rajgarh the top tenth of families earn most of the income; in Sonagarh income is shared more evenly. Which country is likely to have higher welfare? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Same totals; distribution decides welfare.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sonagarh** is likely to have higher welfare. Both have the **same real GDP per head**, but GDP says nothing about **distribution**. An extra rupee adds more to the welfare of a poor family than of a rich one, so a **more even sharing** of the same income meets more basic needs. In Rajgarh, many families may remain poor despite the same average.

questions.stem_md: Explain how non-monetary exchanges and positive externalities make GDP understate the welfare of an imagined rural district.
questions.solution_md: Unpaid activity and unpaid benefits are left out.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Non-monetary exchanges**: much work in the district, such as cooking, child care, kitchen gardens and barter of grain for services, is **not sold for money**, so it is left out of GDP although it adds to welfare.
2. **Positive externalities**: a farmer's orchard that helps neighbours' bees, or a village tank that recharges wells, **benefits others without payment**, so the benefit is not counted.
Both make GDP **understate** welfare.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) What is meant by economic welfare? [2]
(b) "A rise in the real GDP of an imagined country raises its economic welfare." Evaluate this statement with three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Definition; three limitations; balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Economic welfare** is the well-being people get from goods and services that can be **measured in money**, such as food, housing, health care and education.
(b) The statement is **only partly true**. Higher real GDP means more goods and services, which can raise welfare. But (1) **distribution**: if the extra income goes to a few, most people may be no better off; (2) **non-monetary exchanges**: unpaid work and self-produced goods are left out, so GDP may miss welfare changes; (3) **externalities**: pollution from growing industry harms health but is not deducted, while unpaid benefits are not added. So real GDP is a **useful but incomplete** index of welfare.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts. [2 + 2]

(i) For imagined Phalguni Desh, NDP at market price is ₹1,800 crore, indirect taxes ₹90 crore and subsidies ₹150 crore. Find NDP at factor cost.
(ii) Explain why the answer is larger than NDP at market price.
questions.solution_md: Negative net indirect taxes raise factor cost above market price.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Net indirect taxes = 90 − 150 = **-60**. NDP at factor cost = NDP at market price − net indirect taxes = 1800 − (-60) = **₹1,860 crore**.
(ii) Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies. Here **subsidies exceed indirect taxes**, so goods sell **below** what their producers' factors are paid; the government makes up the gap. Removing the negative net indirect taxes therefore **raises** the figure, so factor cost exceeds market price.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about imagined Rewa Desh (₹ crore): GDP at market price 6,000, net factor income from abroad (−) 80, net current transfers from abroad 220, depreciation 500. [2 + 2]

(i) Find gross and net national disposable income.
(ii) Explain why national disposable income can exceed national product.
questions.solution_md: Add transfers to national product; transfers explain the excess.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Gross national disposable income** = GDP at market price + NFIA + net current transfers = 6000 − 80 + 220 = **₹6,140 crore**. **Net** = 6140 − 500 = **₹5,640 crore**.
(ii) Disposable income adds **current transfers from abroad**, such as remittances and gifts, which are not payment for any production at home. When the country receives more transfers than it sends, it can **use more income than it produces**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Net inflow lets use exceed output

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the three items that separate gross from net, market price from factor cost, and domestic from national aggregates.
(ii) Imagined Devgiri reports national income ₹2,700 crore, net factor income from abroad ₹40 crore, depreciation ₹210 crore, indirect taxes ₹330 crore and subsidies ₹50 crore. Find NDP at factor cost, NDP at market price, GDP at market price and GNP at market price.
questions.solution_md: Three adjusting items; four aggregates by reversing them.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Depreciation**, the value of fixed capital used up through wear and tear and expected obsolescence, is subtracted to turn a **gross** aggregate into a **net** one. **Net indirect taxes**, indirect taxes minus subsidies, are subtracted to turn a value at **market price** into one at **factor cost**, because taxes raise and subsidies lower prices without paying any factor. **Net factor income from abroad**, factor income received by normal residents from abroad minus factor income paid to non-residents, is added to turn a **domestic** aggregate into a **national** one.
(ii) **NDP at factor cost** = 2700 − 40 = **₹2,660 crore**. **NDP at market price** = 2660 + (330 − 50) = **₹2,940 crore**. **GDP at market price** = 2940 + 210 = **₹3,150 crore**. **GNP at market price** = 3150 + 40 = **₹3,190 crore**. Each step reverses or applies exactly one of the three items.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Imagined Kesari Ghat's nominal GDP rose from ₹2,000 crore in the base year to ₹2,310 crore, when the GDP deflator was 110. Find real GDP and the real growth rate, and explain why nominal growth overstates the rise in output.
(ii) A minister of Kesari Ghat says the rise in real GDP proves that people are better off. Evaluate this claim.
questions.solution_md: Deflate and compare; evaluate GDP as a welfare index.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Real GDP** = 2310 × 100 ÷ 110 = **₹2,100 crore**. In the base year real GDP equals nominal GDP, 2,000, so **real growth** = (2100 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = **5 per cent**. Nominal GDP rose 15.5 per cent because it is valued at **current prices**: the deflator shows prices rose by 10 per cent, and that price rise inflates nominal GDP without adding goods.
(ii) The claim is **too strong**. More real output can raise welfare, but GDP ignores **how income is distributed**: if gains go to a few, most families may gain little. It leaves out **non-monetary activities** such as unpaid care. It does not deduct **negative externalities** such as pollution from new industry, nor add unpaid benefits. Growth of 5 per cent is a good sign, but welfare must be judged with **other indicators** as well.
